docs.title: RHOAI Multi-Cluster Models-as-a-Service
docs.text:
This guide specifies a consolidated Models-as-a-Service platform on Red Hat OpenShift AI. An Advanced Cluster Management hub in Azure publishes the only AI gateway, and only to the corporate network. Data center 1 serves the flagship large language model on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Data center 2 serves speech, embeddings, and smaller models on NVIDIA L40S PCIe accelerators.

  • Who this guide is for
  • Platform constraints
  • Documentation map

docs.title: Executive track
docs.text: The executive track is written for CIOs, CTOs, infrastructure VPs, and chief AI architects. It covers total cost of ownership for zero-replica failover, service-level tiers, multi-datacenter disaster recovery, and the utilization economics of mixing MIG partitions with time-sliced GPUs.

docs.title: Engineering track
docs.text: The engineering track is written for platform, infrastructure, and MLOps engineers. It provides verbatim command-line procedures and complete Kubernetes manifests for cluster baselines, GPU partitioning, model serving, gateway policy, validation, and operations.

docs.title: Platform constraints
docs.text:
Manifests in this guide follow these rules.

  • The flagship model runs as a single replica. Its pod tolerates node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and node.kubernetes.io/unreachable for 10 seconds.
  • The flagship workload uses priority class flagship-critical-priority with value 1000000000 and preemption policy PreemptLowerPriority.
  • Model weights mount from CephFS persistent volumes with access mode ReadWriteMany.
  • Data center 1 partitions H100 SXM5 GPUs with NVIDIA MIG profiles 3g.40gb and 1g.10gb. Data center 2 shares L40S PCIe GPUs with NVIDIA GPU Operator time-slicing.

docs.title: Executive
docs.text:
• Executive summary covers the hub, the two data centers, and the internal gateway.
  • Business value and TCO covers the four-H100 cost avoidance and the utilization target.
  • SLA and disaster recovery covers flagship failover inside data center 1 and the latency bands.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Global topology covers private links and the flagship failover state machine.
  • Data center 1 H100 covers the Azure virtual machines, MIG layout, and H100 memory bandwidth.
  • Data center 2 L40S covers the on-premises hosts and time-slicing.
  • MaaS gateway covers path routing from the hub.
  • Storage and networking covers local CephFS volumes and the private links.

docs.title: Platform prerequisites
docs.text: OpenShift cluster baselines, OpenShift Data Foundation CephFS ReadWriteMany storage, the NVIDIA GPU Operator, and Kueue queues with the flagship and batch priority classes.

docs.title: GPU partitioning
docs.text: H100 MIG profiles for data center 1, L40S time-slicing for data center 2, and OpenShift AI accelerator profiles that expose those slices to model workloads.

docs.title: Model serving
docs.text: The single-replica flagship inference service, node-failure recovery onto reserved H100 capacity, the smaller-model fleet on L40S, and the speech translation pipeline.

docs.title: MaaS governance
docs.text: The unified Gateway API entry point, Authorino and Kuadrant authentication, request and token rate limits, and self-service API key issuance.

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text: Interactive Jupyter development with idle culling, ad-hoc distributed training on lower-priority GPUs, and model-registry promotion through CI/CD.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: An OpenAI-compatible end-to-end client, failure-injection tests for node loss, and performance benchmarks for the flagship and speech paths.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Node-failure runbooks, DCGM metrics in Prometheus, and a troubleshooting guide for serving, storage, and GPU scheduling faults.

docs.title: Data center 1, H100
docs.text:
Data center 1 is an Azure OpenShift cluster managed by the hub. It has three worker nodes with no GPUs and two Standard_ND96isr_H100_v5 virtual machines. GPU pods schedule only on the two virtual machines.

Each virtual machine provides 96 Intel Xeon Sapphire Rapids vCPUs, 1,900 GiB of memory, and eight NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs. NVLink 4.0 connects those GPUs inside the virtual machine. Each GPU also has a dedicated 400 Gbps NVIDIA Quantum-2 CX7 InfiniBand port. InfiniBand is not the path for flagship tensor parallel. Tensor parallel size 4 stays inside one virtual machine and uses NVLink.

The virtual machines share a size and differ by MIG layout. OpenShift applies that layout with the GPU Operator. This cluster is not an AKS MIG node pool.

Node MIG config Layout GPU node 1 all-disabled GPUs 0-7 remain full H100 devices. The flagship replica uses four of them. GPU node 2 node2-hybrid-profile GPUs 0-3 remain full H100 devices. GPUs 4-7 are MIG-enabled.

Each MIG GPU on node 2 hosts one 3g.40gb instance and four 1g.10gb instances. NVIDIA documents both profile names for the H100 80GB. That mix uses 7 of 7 compute slices and 8 of 8 memory slices. GPUs 0 through 3 stay whole so the flagship can preempt batch work onto four full GPUs without rebuilding MIG geometry during an outage.

The three workers without GPUs run platform services and the OpenShift Data Foundation CephFS volume for this cluster. Both H100 virtual machines mount that volume with ReadWriteMany. Local NVMe on the virtual machines is scratch capacity, not the weight store.

docs.title: Memory bandwidth
docs.text:
NVIDIA publishes these accelerator figures:

Accelerator Memory Bandwidth Link used by the flagship H100 SXM 80GB 80 GB HBM3 3.35 TB/s NVLink, 900 GB/s L40S 48 GB GDDR6 with ECC 864 GB/s PCIe Gen4 x16, 64 GB/s bidirectional

H100 SXM memory bandwidth is about 3.9 times the L40S figure (3.35 TB/s compared with 864 GB/s). With sparsity, NVIDIA publishes 3,958 FP8 teraFLOPS for the H100 SXM and 1,466 FP8 teraFLOPS for the L40S. The flagship uses FP8 for the KV cache on the full H100 GPUs. MIG slices on node 2 do not inherit that flagship argument set.

Sources: NVIDIA H100 product specifications and NVIDIA L40S specifications.

docs.title: Flagship placement
docs.text:
The replica is one pod. Its vLLM process uses --tensor-parallel-size 4, --kv-cache-dtype fp8, --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92, and --max-model-len 32768. It tolerates node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and node.kubernetes.io/unreachable for 10 seconds and runs at flagship-critical-priority.

Node 2 GPUs 4 through 7 remain available to smaller models through the whole failover. Their isolation boundary is the MIG instance, not a second copy of the 72B weights.

docs.title: Data center 2, L40S
docs.text:
Data center 2 is an on-premises OpenShift cluster managed by the hub. It has four bare-metal hosts. Each host has four NVIDIA L40S 48GB PCIe GPUs, for 16 GPUs in the site.

The L40S is not a MIG-capable GPU. NVIDIA lists MIG support as absent for this product, and the card has no NVLink. The GPU Operator shares each GPU with time-slicing: migStrategy is none, and nvidia.com/gpu is advertised at replicas: 4. Sixteen GPUs at four replicas present 64 shared slots.

Time-slicing shares the GPU without the memory and fault isolation MIG provides on the H100. Tenant separation for this site is the hub authentication and quota policy, plus the queue that admits the pod. It is not a hardware memory partition.

docs.title: What runs here
docs.text:
Path Workload /v1/audio/transcriptions Whisper, with vLLM --task transcription /v1/audio/speech Text-to-speech /v1/embeddings Embedding runtime

Whisper and text-to-speech are allowed to scale to zero when idle. The flagship 72B model does not run here. L40S memory is 48 GB of GDDR6 at 864 GB/s, against 80 GB of HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s on the H100 SXM. The interconnect is PCIe Gen4 x16 at 64 GB/s bidirectional.

docs.title: Local weights
docs.text:
OpenShift Data Foundation for this site runs on the four bare-metal hosts, because those are the only nodes in the cluster. Model pods mount that cluster's CephFS volume with ReadWriteMany on StorageClass ocs-storagecluster-cephfs. They do not mount the data center 1 volume across the private link.

The private link to the hub carries inference requests after the gateway has already accepted them. The private link to data center 1 is cluster connectivity, not a weight-serving path.

docs.title: Global topology
docs.text:
Three OpenShift clusters form the platform. The Advanced Cluster Management hub in Azure is the only cluster that publishes the AI gateway. Data center 1 and data center 2 are managed clusters. Private links connect the hub to each data center, and the data centers to each other. Corporate users reach the hub gateway over a private link. The gateway has no internet listener.

flowchart TD
  corp["Corporate network"]
  hub["ACM hub in Azure"]
  dc1["DC1 Azure H100 cluster"]
  dc2["DC2 on-premises L40S cluster"]
  corp -->|"private link"| hub
  hub -->|"private link"| dc1
  hub -->|"private link"| dc2
  dc1 -->|"private link"| dc2
Cluster Where it runs Role ACM hub Azure Cluster management, Gateway API entry, authentication, and rate limits DC1 Azure Flagship 72B model on H100 GPUs, local CephFS weights DC2 On-premises bare metal Speech, text-to-speech, and embeddings on L40S GPUs, local CephFS weights

The hub does not schedule GPU pods and does not store model weights. Inference backends stay on the private links. They are not separately published to the corporate network or to the internet.

Authoring APIs for the later manifests are recorded in the technical schema reference used by the platform and serving authors: InferenceService serving.kserve.io/v1beta1, Gateway and HTTPRoute gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1, and AuthPolicy and RateLimitPolicy kuadrant.io/v1.

docs.title: Request path
docs.text:
A corporate client calls the hub. The hub authenticates the caller and applies the quota for that tier, then forwards the path:

  • /v1/chat/completions to the flagship replica in data center 1.
  • /v1/audio/transcriptions to Whisper in data center 2.
  • /v1/audio/speech to text-to-speech in data center 2.
  • /v1/embeddings to the embedding runtime in data center 2.

The gateway page draws that tree. The storage page explains why the model bytes do not follow those private links on the request path.

docs.title: Flagship failover
docs.text:
Failover is a reschedule inside data center 1. Node 1 serves the replica on four full H100 GPUs. If that virtual machine stays not ready or unreachable for 10 seconds, the scheduler preempts batch work on GPUs 0 through 3 of node 2 and starts the same single replica there. Both virtual machines mount the data center 1 CephFS volume, so the start does not download weights across a private link.

stateDiagram-v2
  direction TB
  [*] --> ServingOnNode1
  ServingOnNode1 --> TolerationWindow: Node 1 is not ready
  TolerationWindow --> ServingOnNode1: Node 1 recovers within 10 seconds
  TolerationWindow --> PreemptBatch: 10 seconds elapse
  PreemptBatch --> ServingOnNode2: GPUs 0 to 3 are freed
  ServingOnNode2 --> ServingOnNode1: Node 1 is ready again

docs.title: Latency bands
docs.text:
• Tensor parallel for the flagship uses NVLink inside one H100 virtual machine. NVIDIA publishes 900 GB/s NVLink for the H100 SXM.
  • Failover uses the two H100 virtual machines and the local CephFS volume in data center 1.
  • Speech and embeddings cross a private link from the hub to data center 2 after the client has already crossed the corporate private link to the hub.

This page does not assign millisecond budgets to those bands.

docs.title: MaaS gateway
docs.text:
The single OpenAI-compatible gateway runs on the Advanced Cluster Management hub in Azure. Corporate clients reach it over a private link. The gateway has no internet listener. Data center inference services are backends on private links. They are not a second public API.

Authentication and rate limits use Connectivity Link 1.4. The authoring API is kuadrant.io/v1 for both AuthPolicy and RateLimitPolicy. kuadrant.io/v1beta2 is rejected. Policies attach to a Gateway API Gateway or HTTPRoute at gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1, which requires Gateway API 1.2 or later on this platform. The policy targetRef.group is gateway.networking.k8s.io.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
The hub is the enforcement point for identity and for request-rate and token-rate tiers. API-key and OIDC authentication both terminate there. A caller who can reach a data center network still needs a policy that allows the path. The gateway is the published contract.

MIG isolation on data center 1 node 2 is independent of the gateway. It limits which GPU memory a smaller model can see. L40S time-slicing does not add that hardware boundary. Quotas on the hub and the queue on the cluster are the controls for that fleet.

Production Gateway, HTTPRoute, AuthPolicy, and RateLimitPolicy manifests belong to the later MaaS governance pages. This page fixes the topology those manifests must implement: one internal listener on the hub, four paths, and private backends.

docs.title: Storage and networking
docs.text: Each workload cluster has its own OpenShift Data Foundation CephFS volume. Pods mount weights only inside their own cluster. The hub does not run that volume. A private link is a cluster-connectivity path, not a Ceph data path for inference.

docs.title: CephFS placement
docs.text:
Cluster Where the volume runs Who mounts it ACM hub No model-weight CephFS Nobody for model weights DC1 Three Azure workers with no GPUs Both H100 virtual machines, access mode ReadWriteMany DC2 Four on-premises bare-metal hosts L40S model pods, access mode ReadWriteMany

The StorageClass on each workload cluster is ocs-storagecluster-cephfs, the default created by a StorageCluster named ocs-storagecluster. Data center 1 uses the three non-GPU workers so the H100 virtual machines are not the Ceph storage nodes. Data center 2 has no separate storage nodes, so the four GPU hosts also host that site's CephFS volume.

Local NVMe on Standard_ND96isr_H100_v5 is scratch. It is not the shared weight store. A flagship failover from node 1 to node 2 mounts the same data center 1 volume the replica already used.

Weights are seeded into each local volume. Serving a model in data center 1 does not read data center 2's Ceph, and the reverse is also true. A stretched Ceph cluster across Azure and the on-premises site would put the inference data path on the private link and would couple the two failure domains. This design keeps those domains separate.

docs.title: Private links
docs.text:
Private links carry cluster traffic:

  • Corporate network to the hub gateway.
  • Hub to data center 1, for the flagship request path.
  • Hub to data center 2, for speech and embeddings.
  • Data center 1 to data center 2, for cluster connectivity between the managed clusters.

The corporate path ends at the hub. Inference services do not listen on the internet, and they are not a second entry point on the corporate network.

docs.title: What stays off the private link
docs.text:
• Flagship tensor parallel, which stays on NVLink inside one H100 virtual machine.
  • Flagship weight reads during failover, which stay on data center 1 CephFS.
  • L40S weight reads, which stay on data center 2 CephFS.

The private link from the hub to data center 2 is on the speech and embedding request path after the gateway accepts the call. It is not on the flagship weight path.

docs.title: Business value and total cost of ownership
docs.text: The platform spends H100 capacity on one serving replica, then reuses the second H100 server for failover and for smaller workloads. L40S servers absorb speech and embeddings. The planning target is sustained GPU use above 80 percent, from MIG partitions on the spare H100s and from time-slicing on every L40S.

docs.title: Zero-replica failover
docs.text:
A hot standby for the flagship would be a second 72B replica on another four H100 GPUs, running at all times. This design keeps a single replica. When the primary Azure virtual machine is lost, the replica moves onto four full H100s that already sit in the second virtual machine. Those four GPUs run preemptable batch work until the flagship needs them.

The planning comparison in this guide values those four avoided H100s at about $140,000 or more of capital or cloud cost. The figure is the cost of the GPUs that a dual-replica design would hold idle for failover. It is not a quote for the whole Azure estate. The two Standard_ND96isr_H100_v5 virtual machines are still required: one for the live replica, one for the failover GPUs, MIG tenants, and batch work.

Weights for that move are already on the data center 1 CephFS volume. Failover does not copy a 72B model across the private link.

docs.title: Where the GPUs go
docs.text:
Pool Hardware Steady-state job Failover job DC1 node 1, four of eight H100s Full GPUs, NVLink inside the virtual machine Flagship 72B replica Returns to this pool when the virtual machine is healthy DC1 node 1, remaining four H100s Full GPUs Other full-GPU work on the same server Stays local to that server DC1 node 2, GPUs 0-3 Full H100s Preemptable batch and training Flagship replica DC1 node 2, GPUs 4-7 MIG 3g.40gb and 1g.10gb Smaller isolated models Stays partitioned DC2, 16 L40S GPUs 4-way time-slicing Speech, text-to-speech, embeddings Stays on premises

Sixteen L40S GPUs with four-way time-slicing present 64 shared GPU slots for the smaller fleet. MIG on the second H100 server packs several smaller models onto GPUs 4 through 7 without giving each of them a full H100.

docs.title: Utilization
docs.text:
MIG is hardware isolation on the H100. A 3g.40gb slice and four 1g.10gb slices fill one 80GB H100, so idle silicon on the failover server still earns its keep. Time-slicing on the L40S lets several speech and embedding pods share one GPU when their duty cycles are bursty. Together, those two sharing modes are how the platform targets more than 80 percent sustained GPU use. That target is a planning objective for scheduling and mix, not a measured production report.

NVIDIA publishes 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 bandwidth for the H100 SXM 80GB and 864 GB/s of GDDR6 bandwidth for the L40S. The flagship stays on the H100 because a 72B model is memory-bandwidth bound. The L40S fleet is the right cost band for the smaller models. The data center 1 page records the comparison.

docs.title: What the hub does not buy
docs.text: The Advanced Cluster Management hub does not carry H100 or L40S GPUs and does not store model weights. Its cost is the control-plane and gateway cluster, not a third GPU estate. Callers still see one internal API, so application teams do not fund a gateway per data center.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
Red Hat OpenShift AI hosts one internal Models-as-a-Service platform for the corporate network. A Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management hub in Azure publishes the only AI gateway. Data center 1, also in Azure, serves the flagship 72B model on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Data center 2, on premises, serves speech, text-to-speech, and embeddings on NVIDIA L40S GPUs.

The gateway is reachable from the corporate network over a private link. It has no internet listener. Private links also connect the hub to each data center, and the two data centers to each other.

flowchart TD
  corp["Corporate network"]
  hub["ACM hub in Azure"]
  dc1["DC1 Azure H100 cluster"]
  dc2["DC2 on-premises L40S cluster"]
  corp -->|"private link"| hub
  hub -->|"private link"| dc1
  hub -->|"private link"| dc2
  dc1 -->|"private link"| dc2

docs.title: What each site is for
docs.text:
The hub is the control and entry cluster. It authenticates callers, applies request and token quotas, and routes OpenAI-compatible paths. It does not run model weights.

Data center 1 keeps one replica of the flagship model on four H100 GPUs inside a single Azure virtual machine. A second, identical virtual machine holds spare full GPUs for failover and smaller MIG-backed workloads. Three additional Azure workers have no GPUs. They carry platform services and the local weight store.

Data center 2 runs Whisper transcription, text-to-speech, and embeddings. Those models share L40S GPUs with time-slicing and can scale to zero when idle.

docs.text:

  stt["/v1/audio/transcriptions"]
  tts["/v1/audio/speech"]
  emb["/v1/embeddings"]

  gw --> tts --> speech

docs.title: Why this shape
docs.text:
One flagship replica avoids paying for a second hot copy of a 72B model. Failover stays inside data center 1, on GPUs that already belong to the platform. Speech and embeddings stay on the less expensive L40S fleet. Callers see one internal /v1 endpoint.

The business value and cost page states the four-H100 saving and the utilization target. The service levels page states the failover and latency bands. The global topology page is the engineering view of the same layout.

docs.title: Service levels and disaster recovery
docs.text: Service levels follow the path a caller uses and the GPU pool behind it. Recovery of the flagship stays inside data center 1. Data center 2 does not become a second home for the 72B model.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text:
Tier Who it serves Protection What can interrupt it Flagship interactive /v1/chat/completions on four H100s Single replica, 10-second node-failure toleration, priority above batch work Loss of DC1 node 1, recovered onto DC1 node 2 Speech and embeddings Audio and embedding paths on L40S GPUs Separate site and local weights; idle replicas may scale to zero DC2 capacity and the private link from the hub Batch and training Preemptable jobs on DC1 node 2 GPUs 0-3 Best effort on GPUs reserved for flagship failover Flagship preemption, without a completion guarantee

The flagship priority class is flagship-critical-priority at value 1000000000, with permission to preempt lower-priority pods. Batch work uses batch-low-priority at value 10000. When node 1 is lost, the flagship takes GPUs 0 through 3 on node 2 and the batch pods on those GPUs stop.

The recovery target exercised by the later node-failure test is restoration of the flagship endpoint in under 60 seconds. The 10-second toleration is the time the scheduler waits before treating the node as gone. It is not, by itself, the full user-visible recovery time.

docs.title: Failover inside data center 1
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  direction TB
  [*] --> ServingOnNode1
  ServingOnNode1 --> TolerationWindow: Node 1 is not ready
  TolerationWindow --> ServingOnNode1: Node 1 recovers within 10 seconds
  TolerationWindow --> PreemptBatch: 10 seconds elapse
  PreemptBatch --> ServingOnNode2: GPUs 0 to 3 are freed
  ServingOnNode2 --> ServingOnNode1: Node 1 is ready again

Both H100 virtual machines mount the same data center 1 CephFS volume. The replica starts on node 2 with weights already local. A private link to data center 2 is not on this recovery path.

Multi-tenant isolation on the spare H100s is MIG. GPUs 4 through 7 stay partitioned as one 3g.40gb instance and four 1g.10gb instances per GPU, including while the flagship occupies GPUs 0 through 3. Callers are isolated at the hub gateway, which is the only published endpoint and which admits only corporate-network clients.

docs.title: Latency bands
docs.text:
The guide does not publish a measured millisecond budget. It distinguishes three bands:

  • Flagship tensor parallel uses NVLink inside one H100 virtual machine.
  • Flagship failover uses the two H100 virtual machines in data center 1, with weights already on that site's CephFS volume.
  • Speech and embeddings travel from the corporate network to the hub, then over a private link to data center 2.

Losing the private link to data center 2 removes speech and embeddings. It does not, by itself, remove the flagship, because that path stays on the hub-to-DC1 private link. Losing the hub, or the corporate private link into the hub, removes every path, because the gateway is the only front door.

docs.title: What disaster recovery does not do
docs.text: Data center 2 is not a flagship disaster-recovery site. L40S memory bandwidth and capacity are the wrong fit for a 72B replica, and the design does not pay for a second hot replica in either site. Weight seeding into each site's own CephFS volume keeps inference off the cross-site link. It is not a stretched storage cluster.
